title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Launches November 5 — New Gameplay Reveals Jumping, Free Camera and More
description: Nintendo has given The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time its biggest remake showcase yet, confirming a November 5, 2026 release date and detailing major gameplay and quality-of-life changes for Switch 2.
body:
Nintendo has finally pulled back the curtain on **The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time** for Nintendo Switch 2, confirming that the remake launches on **November 5, 2026** and showing its most substantial gameplay footage yet during The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct.

The presentation made Nintendo’s direction much clearer: this is a visually rebuilt and mechanically modernized version of the 1998 classic, but one that is deliberately preserving the structure, atmosphere and identity of the original adventure. Series producer **Eiji Aonuma** demonstrated the game during the Direct and described the project as a faithful modernization rather than a wholesale reinvention.

The result is familiar Ocarina of Time with significantly more detailed environments and characters, alongside modern controls and guidance systems that address some of the original game’s biggest age-related friction points.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Official imagery from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Nintendo Switch 2, shown during The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct

contentBlocks.text: Nintendo confirmed that **The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches November 5, 2026**, exclusively for **Nintendo Switch 2**. The remake was first announced in June with only a short teaser and a broad 2026 window; the anniversary Direct is the first time Nintendo has shown the project in extended gameplay and attached a firm release date.
contentBlocks.heading: Ocarina of Time remake release date is November 5

contentBlocks.text: One of the most immediately noticeable gameplay changes is a **free camera**, replacing the far more constrained camera behavior of the Nintendo 64 original. Nintendo has also added a **dedicated jump button**. In the original Ocarina of Time, Link automatically jumped when running off ledges, so giving players direct control over jumping is a meaningful change to how basic traversal feels even if the level layouts remain familiar.
contentBlocks.heading: A free camera and dedicated jump button fundamentally change movement

contentBlocks.text: Nintendo also showed a new guidance feature called **Threads of Time**. The system is intended to help direct players toward their next objective, giving newcomers a clearer path through a game that originally relied heavily on NPC hints, Navi prompts and exploration. It is one of the clearest examples of Nintendo modernizing Ocarina of Time without changing the adventure’s underlying progression.
contentBlocks.heading: Threads of Time is designed to help players find their next objective

contentBlocks.text: The remake adds smaller character-focused touches as well. Nintendo showed that **Link can hum tunes**, reinforcing music as part of the remake’s identity beyond simply using the Ocarina as an item. Aonuma also explained that characters in **Kokiri Village have been given additional lines of dialogue**, making the opening area feel more populated and expressive than it did on Nintendo 64.
contentBlocks.heading: Link can hum melodies, and Kokiri Village has more dialogue

contentBlocks.text: Aonuma discussed the remake’s visual direction during the presentation, explaining that the team wanted something that feels **nostalgic without becoming fully realistic**. The showcase featured dramatically more detailed environments and character models, including a much more imposing **Great Deku Tree**, while retaining the recognizable shapes, locations and fairy-tale atmosphere of the original game. The trailer also showed both Child Link and later portions of the adventure, making clear that this is a full visual reconstruction rather than a simple remaster.
contentBlocks.heading: Nintendo is rebuilding Ocarina of Time’s look without chasing realism

contentBlocks.text: The most important takeaway from Nintendo’s presentation is that the project is not being repositioned as an open-world Zelda in the style of Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom. Aonuma emphasized a **faithful** approach, and the gameplay shown retains the recognizable structure and locations of the original while layering modern controls, navigation help and richer presentation on top. That balance will likely define how longtime players respond to the remake: Nintendo is changing how Ocarina of Time feels to control and inhabit without replacing the game underneath.
contentBlocks.heading: The remake still wants to feel like Ocarina of Time

conclusion: Nintendo’s Zelda 40th Anniversary showcase finally answers the biggest questions surrounding the remake. Ocarina of Time is not being rebuilt into a different kind of Zelda game; Nintendo is preserving the original adventure while modernizing the parts players interact with every minute — movement, camera control, navigation and presentation. With a November 5 release date now locked in, the remaining questions are likely to center on pricing, performance, the extent of any additional content and exactly how much of the original game has been expanded beyond what Nintendo showed today.
conclusionHeading: What Nintendo changed — and what it deliberately kept
